source_title: Beans Production Guide — Tanzania, East Africa

chunks.text: Bean varieties for Tanzania: Common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) — most widely grown. Improved varieties: Lyamungo 85 (red kidney, 90 days to maturity, high yield 1.2-1.8 tons/acre, resistant to angular leaf spot and anthracnose), Jesca (white, 75 days, determinate bush type, good for intercropping), Uyole 94 (red mottled, 80 days, tolerant to bean common mosaic virus), Selian 97 (small white, 85 days, good canning quality). Local varieties: various red and white types, 90-120 days maturity, lower yield 0.5-0.8 tons/acre but adapted to local conditions. Lima bean (Phaseolus lunatus) — larger seed, longer season 100-120 days, drought tolerant. Cowpea (Vigna unguiculata) — dual purpose (grain and leaf vegetable), nitrogen fixing, drought tolerant, 60-90 days for grain, leaves harvested from 30 days.

Bean planting guide for Korogwe: Two seasons — long rains (March-May) and short rains (October-December). Optimal planting: long rains mid-March to mid-April, short rains mid-October to mid-November. Seed rate: 25-30 kg per acre for bush types, 15-20 kg for climbing types. Spacing: bush types 45cm x 15cm (2 seeds per hole), climbing types 60cm x 30cm (2 seeds per hole) with stakes. Planting depth: 3-5cm. Inoculate seeds with Rhizobium for nitrogen fixation (mix with inoculant just before planting). Soil requirements: well-drained, pH 6.0-7.0, sandy loam preferred. Beans do not tolerate waterlogging — avoid poorly drained fields. Fertilizer: apply 50 kg TSP (triple super phosphate) per acre at planting, beans fix their own nitrogen so no nitrogen fertilizer needed. Intercropping: beans intercrop well with maize (plant 1 row beans between 2 rows maize), cassava, and sorghum.

Bean pests in Tanzania: Bean fly (Ophiomyia spp) — larvae mine stems causing wilting and death of seedlings, most damaging pest in East Africa, control: seed treatment with imidacloprid, early planting to avoid peak fly activity, destroy crop residues. Bean stem maggot — similar damage to bean fly, larvae tunnel into stems. Aphids (Aphis fabae) — transmit bean common mosaic virus, cause leaf curling and reduced yield, control: spray with dimethoate 40EC at 20ml per 20L, or neem-based products. Flower thrips (Megalurothrips sjostedti) — feed on flowers causing flower abortion and flat pods, control: spray with lambda-cyhalothrin at flowering. Pod borers (Maruca vitrata) — larvae feed on flowers and pods, webbing visible, control: spray with Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) or lambda-cyhalothrin at flowering and podding. Bruchids (Callosobruchus maculatus) — post-harvest storage pest, adults bore into stored beans, control: hermetic storage (PICS bags), or treat stored beans with diatomaceous earth.

Bean diseases in Tanzania: Angular leaf spot (Phaeoisariopsis griseola) — brown angular lesions on leaves, premature defoliation, seed-borne, control: resistant varieties (Lyamungo 85), crop rotation (3 years), certified seed. Bean common mosaic virus (BCMV) — transmitted by aphids, leaf mosaic and distortion, seed-borne, control: resistant varieties, control aphids, certified virus-free seed. Anthracnose (Colletotrichum lindemuthianum) — dark sunken lesions on pods and stems, seed-borne, control: resistant varieties, crop rotation, certified seed. Root rot (Fusarium solani, Rhizoctonia solani) — wilting and root decay, favored by waterlogging, control: well-drained fields, crop rotation, avoid continuous bean cropping. Bacterial blight (Xanthomonas axonopodis) — water-soaked lesions on leaves, angular leaf spot appearance, control: resistant varieties, avoid overhead irrigation, crop rotation.

Bean harvest and post-harvest: Harvest when 80-90% of pods are dry and brown (90-120 days after planting). Pull entire plant and stack upright in field for 3-5 days to dry further. Thresh by beating dried plants with sticks on clean ground or in sacks. Winnow to remove chaff. Dry grain to 12-13% moisture for safe storage (bite test: should shatter, not dent). Storage: use hermetic bags (PICS bags) to prevent bruchid damage, or treat with diatomaceous earth at 0.5% by weight. Store in cool dry place off the ground. Yield benchmarks: low input (local variety, no fertilizer): 0.4-0.6 tons per acre. Medium input (improved variety, TSP, Rhizobium): 0.8-1.2 tons per acre. High input (improved variety, fertilizer, pest control, irrigation): 1.5-2.0 tons per acre. Bean value chain: sell as dry grain to local markets, or for export (large white and red kidney beans fetch premium prices), or process into canned beans.
